nodes.label: Perko systems researchers network
nodes.description: An incomplete 2026 community network of systems thinkers and cyberneticians. It is retained as a comparator whose inclusions, omissions and edge meanings require reconstruction and source checking.

nodes.label: Adaptation
nodes.description: Adaptation is relational: change is adaptive only with respect to some environment, timescale and viability condition. Local adjustment can make the larger system more fragile.
nodes.canonical_definition: Change in a system's organisation, behaviour or relations that improves or preserves its capacity to remain viable in a changing environment.

nodes.label: Autonomy
nodes.description: Autonomy is not independence. A viable part needs discretion, information and resources, while remaining connected to wider identity and constraints.
nodes.canonical_definition: The operational freedom and regulatory capacity of a part to respond to its local environment without being reduced to a passive execution point of the whole.

nodes.label: Boundaries
nodes.description: Alternative plural label for Boundary. Public search resolves this entry to the canonical Boundary page.

nodes.label: Boundary
nodes.description: A boundary makes inquiry and action possible by limiting what must be handled at once. It also externalises people, effects and responsibilities. Good systems work therefore treats boundary choice as practical, political and ethical.
nodes.canonical_definition: A purpose- and observer-dependent distinction that marks what is treated as inside, outside or marginal to a system of concern and thereby shapes explanation, legitimacy and intervention.

nodes.label: Chaos
nodes.description: In mathematics and complexity science, chaos is deterministic behaviour that can be highly sensitive to initial conditions and difficult to predict over time. It is not the same as randomness or mere disorder.

nodes.label: Cohesion
nodes.description: Cohesion connects differentiated parts without erasing their local variety. It is produced through identity, coordination, shared constraints, mutual information and conflict handling.
nodes.canonical_definition: The degree of integration, mutual constraint and common identity through which autonomous parts remain capable of acting as a whole.

nodes.label: Complexity
nodes.description: Complexity concerns the variety, interaction, interdependence and change that make a situation hard to describe, predict or regulate. What counts as complex depends partly on the observer, purpose, scale and available model.

nodes.label: Difference
nodes.description: A difference is a distinguishable contrast between possible states, descriptions or relations. Systems and cybernetics ask which differences an observer can detect and which can alter subsequent action.

nodes.label: Distinction
nodes.description: Distinctions make a world manageable enough for thought and action. They do not merely copy divisions already waiting in reality; they select, stabilise and test differences for a purpose.
nodes.canonical_definition: A situated act of marking a difference so that one side can be indicated, discussed or acted upon; the distinction reveals some possibilities and leaves others unmarked.

nodes.label: Double bind
nodes.description: A double bind is a recurring communication situation in which a person receives incompatible injunctions at different logical levels and cannot safely comment on or leave the situation. The term is strongly associated with Gregory Bateson and colleagues.

nodes.label: Double-loop learning
nodes.description: Double-loop learning changes not only an action but the governing assumptions, values or rules by which the action was chosen. It is distinguished from correcting performance while leaving those rules intact.

nodes.label: Dynamics
nodes.description: Dynamics is the study of how states, relationships or patterns change over time, including the processes that generate trajectories, cycles, growth, decline or stability.

nodes.label: Dynamics of loops
nodes.description: The dynamics of loops concerns how interacting reinforcing and balancing feedback processes, delays and non-linearities combine to produce behaviour over time.

nodes.label: Emergence
nodes.description: The appearance at one scale of properties, patterns or capacities not straightforwardly present at another scale, arising through interactions and organisation. It describes a relation across levels; it is not a hidden causal substance.
nodes.canonical_definition: A relation across levels or scales in which a macro-property or pattern arises from interactions among lower-level components yet is not usefully reducible to a simple inventory of those components.

nodes.label: Feedback
nodes.description: A family of circular causal or informational relations in which consequences return to influence later state or action. Its sign, delay, reference condition, mechanism and response capacity must be stated.
nodes.canonical_definition: A circular causal or informational relation in which an output or consequence affects later input, state or action. The sign, delay, reference condition and mechanism must be stated.

nodes.label: Feedback loops
nodes.description: A feedback loop is a closed chain of influence in which a consequence returns to affect a later cause or decision. This public entry resolves to the broader canonical Feedback page.

nodes.label: Feedforward
nodes.description: Anticipatory action based on a desired future, a measured disturbance or a model of likely effects, taken before the resulting output is available for correction.
nodes.canonical_definition: A control or coordination relation in which information about intended conditions or measured disturbances is used to act before the resulting output is observed; effectiveness depends on the adequacy of the model or prediction.

nodes.label: Fractals
nodes.description: Fractals are mathematical or spatial structures showing patterned detail across scales, often through self-similarity or scale invariance. Organisational recursion and fractal geometry should not be treated as synonyms.

nodes.label: Holism
nodes.description: Holism studies a phenomenon through the organisation and relations of the whole, not only through isolated parts. It does not require claiming that everything is connected to everything else in the same way.

nodes.label: Homeostasis
nodes.description: Dynamic maintenance or restoration of internal variables within viable ranges despite disturbance. It is neither immobility nor a synonym for a single feedback loop.
nodes.canonical_definition: The organised maintenance of internal variables within viable ranges despite disturbance; the relevant variables, ranges, mechanisms and time scales must be specified.

nodes.label: Identity
nodes.description: Identity is continuity through change, not the absence of change. It is enacted through boundaries, narratives, roles, purposes, memory and repeated relations.
nodes.canonical_definition: A maintained pattern of distinctions, relationships and commitments through which a system remains recognisable across adaptation without requiring unchanging components.

nodes.label: Information
nodes.description: Information is not raw stuff that flows unchanged through channels. A signal becomes information only within some receiving organisation, code, concern or capacity to respond.
nodes.canonical_definition: A difference selected and taken up within an organised context so that it can alter expectation, state or action; its mathematical measure is distinct from meaning and use.

nodes.label: Information theory
nodes.description: A mathematical theory of communication and uncertainty. Shannon information concerns the selection and transmission of possibilities under probability and noise; it does not by itself supply semantic meaning or value.
nodes.canonical_definition: The mathematical study of the quantification, coding and reliable transmission of uncertainty-bearing signals, including entropy, channel capacity, redundancy and noise.

nodes.label: Interrelationships
nodes.description: Interrelationships are the dependencies, influences and mutual constraints through which elements affect one another and contribute to the behaviour of a wider whole.

nodes.label: Modelling
nodes.description: Modelling is the purposeful construction and use of a selective representation. A model makes some distinctions useful for a question while omitting others; it should be judged in relation to its purpose, not mistaken for the world itself.

nodes.label: Multiple perspectives
nodes.description: Multiple perspectives work compares how different participants or observers define the situation, its boundaries, purposes, evidence and possible actions. The differences are evidence, not noise to be averaged away automatically.

nodes.label: Negative feedback
nodes.description: A returned effect that counteracts deviation or change. It often supports regulation and stability, but excessive gain or delay can also create oscillation or instability.
nodes.canonical_definition: A feedback relation in which the returned effect opposes a change or deviation in the relevant variable; the reference condition, loop gain, delay and mechanism must be specified.

nodes.label: Networks
nodes.description: A network represents entities as nodes and relationships as links. Network analysis studies patterns such as connectivity, centrality, clustering, paths and diffusion, while remembering that the chosen nodes and links are modelling decisions.

nodes.label: Non-linearity
nodes.description: A relation is non-linear when effects do not change in simple proportion to causes and the combined effect cannot be inferred by adding isolated effects. Thresholds, saturation and interacting feedback often create non-linearity.

nodes.label: Observer
nodes.description: The observer is not an optional spectator outside the system. Sensors, language, history, interests and position shape what becomes signal, object, boundary and possible action.
nodes.canonical_definition: A situated participant in knowing and acting whose capacities and distinctions partly constitute the world available for description and intervention.

nodes.label: Organisational recursion
nodes.description: A domain-specific use of recursion in which operational units may themselves be treated as viable systems with corresponding requirements at another level. Visual nesting alone is not enough.
nodes.canonical_definition: A domain-specific use of recursion in which an organisational system contains operational units that may themselves be treated as systems with structurally corresponding viability requirements at another level.

nodes.label: Positive feedback
nodes.description: A feedback relation in which returned effects reinforce the direction of change. It can amplify, switch, latch, tip or oscillate depending on loop gain, delay, saturation and constraints.
nodes.canonical_definition: A feedback relation in which the returned effect reinforces rather than counteracts a change in the relevant variable; the sign, loop gain, delay and limiting conditions must be specified.

nodes.label: Purpose
nodes.description: Purpose may be declared, negotiated, inferred from behaviour or attributed by an observer. These forms can conflict. Systems practice needs the conflict visible rather than forcing one slogan to do all the work.
nodes.canonical_definition: A context-dependent orientation or attribution that makes some outcomes, distinctions and actions relevant and supplies criteria for judging performance or viability.

nodes.label: Purposeful behaviour
nodes.description: Behaviour treated in the Rosenblueth–Wiener–Bigelow scheme through observable input/output relations and teleological organisation, with negative feedback central to a major class of purposive mechanisms.
nodes.canonical_definition: A source-specific concept: behaviour classified as oriented towards an end state or goal; in the 1943 scheme, feedback is used to distinguish important classes of purposive behaviour.

nodes.label: Randomness
nodes.description: Randomness describes outcomes treated as not deterministically predictable within a model and represented probabilistically. It should be distinguished from ignorance, measurement error and deterministic chaos.

nodes.label: Recursion
nodes.description: A family of relations in which a definition, operation, organisation or observation is reapplied to instances of the same kind. The domain, recurrence rule and boundary condition must be stated.
nodes.canonical_definition: A family of domain-specific relations in which a definition, operation, structure or organisation is reapplied to instances of the same kind. A conforming account must state the domain, recurrence rule and boundary or termination condition; organisational recursion is not automatically computational recursion or visual self-similarity.

nodes.label: Recursive computation
nodes.description: An algorithmic procedure in which a function calls itself on a smaller part of a task until a base case is reached.
nodes.canonical_definition: A computational procedure in which an operation invokes an instance of itself on a reduced problem and terminates through one or more base cases.

nodes.label: Recursive definition
nodes.description: A definition that determines a value or structure using the same function or form on smaller, simpler or previously defined arguments, normally with a base condition.
nodes.canonical_definition: A definition in which instances of a function or structure are specified in terms of the same function or structure on smaller or prior arguments, together with a base condition or well-founded rule.

nodes.label: Regulation
nodes.description: The constraint of possible outcomes under disturbance in relation to specified goals, essential variables or acceptable states. Regulation can use feedback, feedforward, structure, constraint or combinations of them.
nodes.canonical_definition: A relation among disturbances, a reguland, a regulator and acceptable outcomes in which outcome variety is constrained relative to a stated goal or essential-variable range.

nodes.label: Relating
nodes.description: Relating is a systems-thinking practice of attending to connections, mutual effects, context and patterns between things rather than treating objects as self-contained units.

nodes.label: Requisite variety
nodes.description: The regulatory requirement and limit expressed by Ashby: reducing outcome variety depends on the regulator having usable discriminations and responses relative to disturbances and constraints.
nodes.canonical_definition: The variety needed in a regulator, given disturbances, transformations and acceptable outcomes, to achieve the intended reduction in outcome variety. It is a limit on regulation, not a general instruction to maximise complication.

nodes.label: Self-organisation
nodes.description: The development of global order or coordination through local interactions without an external central controller specifying the resulting pattern. Boundaries, constraints, energy and environment still matter.
nodes.canonical_definition: A process in which interactions among components generate or maintain an organised macro-pattern without a central external controller prescribing that pattern; the system boundary, local rules, constraints and environment must be specified.

nodes.label: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions
nodes.description: Sensitive dependence occurs when very small differences in starting conditions grow into large differences in later trajectories. It is a defining feature of many chaotic dynamical systems.

nodes.label: Single-loop learning
nodes.description: Single-loop learning detects and corrects a mismatch while leaving the governing goals, values or rules intact. It improves action within the current frame rather than questioning the frame itself.

nodes.label: Transduction
nodes.description: Transduction explains why a citizen's life becomes a case, a need becomes a code, work becomes a metric and strategy becomes a local instruction. The message is changed by the receiving world's categories and capacities.
nodes.canonical_definition: A boundary process that transforms signals, meanings or varieties from one domain into a form another domain can register and act upon; it is never assumed to be lossless.

nodes.label: Uncertainty
nodes.description: Uncertainty is the limited ability to know which state, explanation or outcome applies. It can arise from incomplete information, ambiguity, model limits, stochastic variation or changing conditions.

nodes.label: Unpredictability
nodes.description: Unpredictability is the inability to make a sufficiently reliable forecast at a specified horizon and resolution. It may arise from missing knowledge, randomness, sensitivity, emergence or limits of computation and observation.

nodes.label: Variety
nodes.description: The number of distinguishable possibilities in a specified set. Variety depends on which distinctions are available to an observer for a purpose; it is not a synonym for vague complexity.
nodes.canonical_definition: The number of distinguishable elements or possible states in a specified set, sometimes expressed logarithmically; the distinctions and observer must be stated.

nodes.label: Variety amplification
nodes.description: Amplification expands what a system can notice or do through capability, discretion, tools, coordination, networks and access to resources.
nodes.canonical_definition: A deliberate increase in effective sensing or response variety available to a regulator, channel or operational unit.

nodes.label: Variety attenuation
nodes.description: Attenuation protects a regulator from being overwhelmed. It can simplify, buffer, aggregate or redesign demand. It can also erase inconvenient people and conditions if the boundary and purpose are wrong.
nodes.canonical_definition: A deliberate reduction in effective variety so that relevant disturbances, signals or choices become tractable without pretending the discarded variety never existed.

nodes.label: Viability
nodes.description: Viability is not short-term survival or financial solvency. It concerns whether a system can keep producing itself as a coherent actor while its environment and internal conditions change.
nodes.canonical_definition: The capacity of a system to continue as a recognisable whole by balancing present operations, regulation, learning, adaptation and identity under changing conditions.

nodes.label: Action learning
nodes.description: Action learning brings a small group together to work on real problems through questioning, action and reflection. The problem, the learner and the group process are all treated as sources of learning.

nodes.label: Action research
nodes.description: Action research combines inquiry and practical change in repeated cycles of action, observation and reflection, with participants involved in producing the knowledge used.

nodes.label: Agile project management
nodes.description: Agile project management organises work through short feedback cycles, incremental delivery, prioritisation and adaptation rather than relying on a fully fixed plan made in advance.

nodes.label: Appreciative Inquiry
nodes.description: Appreciative Inquiry explores strengths, valued experience and desired possibilities as material for collective change, commonly through cycles of discovery, dream, design and delivery or destiny.

nodes.label: Coaching
nodes.description: Coaching is a structured helping relationship that supports a person or group to examine goals, assumptions, options, practice and learning without simply supplying expert answers.

nodes.label: Constellations
nodes.description: Systemic constellations use spatial representation and embodied positioning to explore perceived relationships within a system. Interpretations should be treated as hypotheses, not objective readings of hidden reality.

nodes.label: Conversation mapping
nodes.description: Conversation mapping makes the structure and content of dialogue visible so that questions, commitments, disagreements, assumptions and unresolved issues can be examined together.

nodes.label: Covert operations
nodes.description: Covert processes are unofficial, hidden or indirect activities through which organisational change is advanced or resisted. Their ethical and political implications require explicit scrutiny.

nodes.label: Critical Social Learning Systems
nodes.description: Critical social learning systems examine how groups learn together while questioning power, boundaries, institutions and the conditions under which some knowledge is admitted or excluded.

nodes.label: Culture mapping
nodes.description: Culture mapping surfaces recurring stories, symbols, routines, power structures, controls and assumptions that shape how an organisation interprets and acts.

nodes.label: Data analysis including SPC and statistics
nodes.description: Data analysis uses quantitative evidence to distinguish patterns, variation and uncertainty. Statistical process control is particularly concerned with behaviour over time and the difference between common and special causes of variation.

nodes.label: Decision structure design
nodes.description: Decision structure design clarifies which decisions exist, what information they require, who should take them, how they interact and how consequences return as learning.

nodes.label: Deming
nodes.description: Deming's management approach joins appreciation for a system, knowledge of variation, theory of knowledge and psychology in a critique of target-driven, blame-based and locally optimised management.

nodes.label: Detecting and managing undiscussables
nodes.description: Work on undiscussables identifies issues people cannot safely raise and the defensive routines that keep both the issue and its unmentionability in place.

nodes.label: Facilitation
nodes.description: Facilitation designs and supports a group process so participants can do purposeful work together while the facilitator attends to participation, power, task, relationships and learning.

nodes.label: Flawless consulting
nodes.description: Flawless Consulting is Peter Block's approach to contracting, diagnosis, feedback and implementation in ways that preserve honesty, shared responsibility and the client's ownership of action.

nodes.label: Fractal Enterprise Model and Capabilities
nodes.description: The Fractal Enterprise Model represents recurring relationships between organisational capabilities and the contexts that enable or constrain them, supporting analysis across scales.

nodes.label: Graphic facilitation and visualisation
nodes.description: Graphic facilitation uses live or prepared visual representation to help groups see relationships, retain contributions, compare interpretations and build shared working models.

nodes.label: Iceberg model
nodes.description: The iceberg model invites inquiry below visible events into patterns, structures and sometimes underlying assumptions. It is a prompt for deeper investigation, not a proof that one hidden cause exists.

nodes.label: Influence mapping
nodes.description: Influence mapping represents actors, decisions, resources and relationships that may shape an issue, helping users examine formal and informal routes of influence.

nodes.label: Influencing and mediation
nodes.description: Influencing and mediation help parties understand interests, differences, options and relationships so that movement becomes possible without pretending conflict has disappeared.

nodes.label: Interview technique
nodes.description: Interview technique covers the design and conduct of conversations that elicit experience, evidence, meaning and disagreement while limiting leading questions and premature interpretation.

nodes.label: Ladder of abstraction
nodes.description: The ladder of abstraction helps people move between concrete observations and broader categories or principles, checking where meaning or evidence changes along the way.

nodes.label: Ladder of inference
nodes.description: The ladder of inference shows how people move from selected observations through interpretation and assumption to conclusions and action, often without noticing the intermediate steps.

nodes.label: Large group decision approaches
nodes.description: Large-group decision approaches structure participation, dialogue and synthesis so many people can contribute to consequential choices without reducing the process to a sequence of speeches.

nodes.label: Large group engagement processes
nodes.description: Large-group engagement processes such as Open Space, World Café and Future Search create different conditions for broad participation, connection, inquiry and commitment.

nodes.label: Lean and Six Sigma
nodes.description: Lean focuses on flow, value and the removal of avoidable work; Six Sigma focuses on variation and defect reduction. Both can support systemic improvement or become narrow efficiency programmes when purpose and boundary are poorly chosen.

nodes.label: Learning design and learning conversations
nodes.description: Learning design creates conditions, activities and feedback through which people can develop capability. Learning conversations make experience, interpretation, practice and next action discussable.

nodes.label: Linear argument technique
nodes.description: Linear argument technique sets out a claim and the chain of reasons and evidence supporting it. It is useful for clarity but should not be mistaken for a complete representation of a complex situation.

nodes.label: Listening and multiple perspectives
nodes.description: Listening for multiple perspectives seeks not only different opinions but the distinct experiences, boundaries, purposes and assumptions from which those accounts make sense.

nodes.label: Managing deflection, resistance and challenge
nodes.description: This practice attends to avoidance, defensive routines, disagreement and refusal without treating every objection as pathology or every change proposal as inherently legitimate.

nodes.label: Metaphors
nodes.description: Metaphors organise attention by making one domain intelligible through another. They reveal and conceal at the same time, so systems practitioners compare metaphors rather than treating one as literal truth.

nodes.label: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
nodes.description: Neuro-Linguistic Programming is a collection of communication and change techniques developed in the 1970s. Its broad theoretical and therapeutic claims are contested and should be separated from any specific practice being evaluated.

nodes.label: Presentation design
nodes.description: Presentation design selects and arranges words, images, sequence and interaction so an audience can follow an argument, inspect evidence and retain the distinctions that matter.

nodes.label: Productive conversations
nodes.description: Productive conversations make observations, interpretations, concerns, requests, commitments and learning explicit enough for people to coordinate action and examine disagreement.

nodes.label: Public speaking
nodes.description: Public speaking is the design and delivery of spoken communication for an audience, including argument, explanation, narrative, evidence, presence and response to the room.

nodes.label: Questionnaire design
nodes.description: Questionnaire design turns an inquiry into answerable questions and response formats while managing ambiguity, bias, burden, sampling and the limits of what self-report can establish.

nodes.label: Scientific theory and evidence
nodes.description: Scientific theory and evidence concern how explanations generate testable expectations, how observations bear on claims, and how uncertainty, replication and rival accounts are handled.

nodes.label: Selling systems approaches
nodes.description: Selling systems approaches means helping sponsors understand the problem the approach addresses, the work and uncertainty involved, and what it can and cannot promise, rather than disguising it as a guaranteed technique.

nodes.label: Stakeholder analysis
nodes.description: Stakeholder analysis identifies people and groups affected by or able to affect an issue, while examining interests, power, legitimacy, relationships and who has been omitted by the chosen boundary.

nodes.label: Training design
nodes.description: Training design specifies the capability to be developed, the practice and feedback needed, the learning sequence, accessibility and how transfer into real work will be supported and assessed.

nodes.label: Transactional Analysis
nodes.description: Transactional Analysis is a psychological and communication framework associated with Eric Berne, using concepts such as ego states, transactions, games and scripts to examine recurring interaction patterns.

nodes.label: Trust mapping and metrics
nodes.description: Trust mapping examines where reliance, confidence and vulnerability sit in a system. Metrics can inform this inquiry but cannot reduce trust to a single context-free score.

nodes.label: Values mapping and integration
nodes.description: Values mapping surfaces what different people or groups treat as worth protecting or pursuing, including conflicts and trade-offs that cannot be resolved by listing agreeable words.

nodes.label: Vanguard Method
nodes.description: The Vanguard Method studies public and service organisations from the outside in, using demand, purpose, flow and measures to redesign work around what matters to service users.

nodes.label: Verbal Behaviours (Rackham)
nodes.description: Rackham's verbal-behaviour work classifies observable contributions in meetings and negotiations, helping practitioners examine how questions, proposals, support, disagreement and summarising affect interaction.

nodes.label: Workshop design
nodes.description: Workshop design creates a bounded social process with a clear purpose, participants, sequence, activities, information, decision rights and follow-through rather than merely filling an agenda with exercises.

nodes.label: Adams' Third Law
nodes.description: Adams' Third Law warns that selecting components because each appears low-risk in isolation can create a high-risk system. Systemic risk depends on fit, interdependence and context, not merely on the local reliability of parts.

nodes.label: Complexity Instability Principle
nodes.description: The Complexity Instability Principle says that systems with too many active or changing interdependencies tend towards instability. Appropriate grouping, modularity and constraints can reduce the number of relationships that must change together.

nodes.label: Conant-Ashby Theorem
nodes.description: The Conant–Ashby theorem states, under the assumptions of the original formal paper, that the simplest optimal regulator must embody a model of what it regulates. Popular uses should not erase those assumptions or turn every useful representation into a proof of optimal control.
nodes.canonical_definition: Under the 1970 paper's explicit assumptions and entropy-minimising criterion, the simplest optimal regulator's actions are mapped versions of the reguland's events. The theorem does not license every popular claim about internal models.

nodes.label: Conservation of Adaptation Principle
nodes.description: The Conservation of Adaptation Principle says that continued existence requires ongoing change in the relationship between a system and its environment. What a system is cannot be separated entirely from the environment in which it persists.

nodes.label: Darkness Principle
nodes.description: The Darkness Principle says that no system can be known completely. Models are therefore necessary selective constructions, and responsible intervention requires explicit uncertainty rather than a pretence of exhaustive knowledge.

nodes.label: Feedback Dominance Theorem
nodes.description: The Feedback Dominance Theorem says that sufficiently strong feedback can dominate system behaviour across substantial variation in initial input. In such cases, changing the input alone may have little effect on the resulting trajectory.

nodes.label: First Black Box Principle
nodes.description: The First Black Box Principle says that it is not always necessary to know a sub-system's internal mechanism in order to understand the function it performs, provided its relevant conditions, inputs and outputs are sufficiently reliable.

nodes.label: First Circular Causality Principle
nodes.description: The First Circular Causality Principle concerns positive feedback. Mutually amplifying changes can drive escalation, so similar initial conditions may lead to radically different outcomes once reinforcing loops take hold.

nodes.label: Fractal Principle
nodes.description: The Fractal Principle proposes that systems tend to reproduce aspects of their own form when they create sub-systems. The claim concerns recurring organisational pattern; it should not be confused with exact mathematical fractal geometry.

nodes.label: Homeostasis Principle
nodes.description: The Homeostasis Principle says that a system remains stable only while its essential variables stay within viable limits. Regulation is therefore concerned with keeping those variables inside a tolerable range, not freezing the system in one exact state.

nodes.label: Law of Calling
nodes.description: The Law of Calling says that identifying a system requires drawing a distinction: a boundary separates what is being treated as the system from its environment. The chosen name and boundary shape what can then be noticed and acted upon.

nodes.label: Law of Crossing
nodes.description: The Law of Crossing says that crossing a system boundary changes state and viewpoint. Defining or observing a system from inside is not equivalent to doing so from outside, and each position permits some distinctions while excluding others.

nodes.label: Law of Reciprocity of Connections
nodes.description: The Law of Reciprocity of Connections says that relationships should be examined as mutual rather than one-way: if A acts on B, B's response changes the situation for A. Actions in connected systems return as consequences.

nodes.label: Law of Requisite Variety
nodes.description: The Law of Requisite Variety limits what regulation can achieve: only regulatory variety can counter disturbance variety. The relevant varieties depend on the defined regulation problem, available responses and acceptable outcomes.
nodes.canonical_definition: For a specified regulation problem, the achievable reduction in outcome variety is bounded by the variety available through the regulator; the original formulation is conditional and relational, not simply 'controller complexity must exceed system complexity'.

nodes.label: Law of Sufficient Complexity
nodes.description: The Law of Sufficient Complexity says that a complex system's behaviour follows from how the system is constituted. Reliable change in behaviour usually requires change to structure, relationships, constraints or inputs, not exhortation alone.

nodes.label: Network Power Law
nodes.description: The Network Power Law draws attention to the rapid growth of possible relationships as the number of elements increases. Connectivity may create utility, but it also produces structural complexity faster than simple element counts suggest.

nodes.label: Order Osmosis Principle
nodes.description: The Order Osmosis Principle proposes that, where more and less organised systems sit beside one another, people, resources or functions tend to migrate towards the more ordered system. This can further weaken the less stable neighbour.

nodes.label: Power Structuration Theorem
nodes.description: The Power Structuration Theorem says that agency must be balanced across recursive levels. A whole needs enough power to act as a whole, while its constituent sub-systems need enough autonomy to meet the demands that fall on them.

nodes.label: Principle of Emergence
nodes.description: The Principle of Emergence concerns properties or behaviours of a whole that are not properties of its parts in isolation. Understanding them requires attention to organisation, interaction and level, not only decomposition.

nodes.label: Redundancy of Potential Command Principle
nodes.description: The Redundancy of Potential Command Principle says that effective action in a complex decision network depends on bringing the right information together where and when it is needed. Command potential is therefore distributed rather than fixed permanently in one role.

nodes.label: Relaxation Time Principle
nodes.description: The Relaxation Time Principle says that a system repeatedly disturbed before it has recovered may never stabilise. The interval between disturbances therefore matters as much as the severity of each disturbance.

nodes.label: Root Structuring Theorem
nodes.description: The Root Structuring Theorem proposes that structural complexity can be reduced by grouping elements into a balanced number of sub-systems at successive levels, with the square-root relationship offered as a guide rather than a universal organisation chart.

nodes.label: Scaling Stasis Principle
nodes.description: The Scaling Stasis Principle says that growth usually adds environmental exposure, internal interdependence and constraints. As a system becomes larger and more complex, those constraints can reduce its capacity to adapt.

nodes.label: Second Black Box Principle
nodes.description: The Second Black Box Principle says that the possible variety of a sub-system's outputs can sometimes be assessed without opening the box. This permits selective modelling, but only under the conditions for which the observed behaviour holds.

nodes.label: Second Circular Causality Principle
nodes.description: The Second Circular Causality Principle concerns negative feedback. Mutual correction can drive a system towards an equilibrium across a wide range of starting conditions; the resulting stability may be desirable or obstructive.

nodes.label: Self-Organised Criticality
nodes.description: Self-Organised Criticality describes systems whose own interactions accumulate tensions or dependencies that make abrupt reorganisation or collapse increasingly likely. The critical condition is produced within the system rather than imposed only from outside.

nodes.label: Self-Organising Principle
nodes.description: The Self-Organising Principle concerns the generation of higher-level order through interactions among parts, and the continuing reorganisation of an existing whole. It is not merely a synonym for teams managing themselves.

nodes.label: Steady State Principle
nodes.description: The Steady State Principle links the equilibrium of a system to the equilibria of its sub-systems and vice versa. A steady state is a maintained dynamic balance, not motionless stasis.

nodes.label: Structural Viability Theorem
nodes.description: The Structural Viability Theorem says that a system and its constituent sub-systems need rates of change fitted to their respective environments. Viability suffers when one recursive level cannot change at the pace demanded of it.

nodes.label: System Resonance Principle
nodes.description: The System Resonance Principle proposes that communication and relation are easier where systems share relevant structural or dynamic similarities. Where those similarities are absent, signals are more likely to be lost or transformed in translation.

nodes.label: System Stability Principle
nodes.description: The System Stability Principle says that something is recognisable as a system only when a pattern of relationships persists across repeated observations. Stability here means persistence of pattern, not the absence of movement.

nodes.label: System Survival Theorem
nodes.description: The System Survival Theorem says that a system cannot remain viable indefinitely if its relevant environment changes consistently faster than the system can adapt. The comparison must be made at a stated scale and time horizon.

nodes.label: Viability Principle
nodes.description: The Viability Principle treats continued existence as a dynamic balance: sub-systems need enough autonomy while the whole retains cohesion, and the system needs enough stability while remaining able to adapt over time.

nodes.label: Agent-based modelling
nodes.description: Agent-based modelling simulates heterogeneous agents following specified rules and interacting in an environment, allowing collective patterns to develop from local behaviour.

nodes.label: Bubble Strategy
nodes.description: The Bubble Strategy is an approach to organisational change in which protected, defensible pockets of new practice are allowed to develop before wider assessment or adoption.

nodes.label: Confrontation Analysis (CONAN)
nodes.description: Confrontation Analysis is a structured approach to dilemmas, positions and potential interactions in conflict or negotiation. It develops from drama theory and helps participants examine how commitments and options may change.

nodes.label: Critical Systems Heuristics (CSH)
nodes.description: Critical Systems Heuristics is a framework for examining the boundary judgements built into plans and interventions: who benefits, who decides, what counts as expertise, and who or what is left outside.

nodes.label: INFORMED Group Dynamics
nodes.description: INFORMED Group Dynamics is included from the SCiO competency corpus. A reliable public explanation and openly accessible source are still required before this entry is treated as complete.

nodes.label: Interactive Management
nodes.description: Interactive Management is a facilitated group process associated with John Warfield and Alexander Christakis. It combines structured dialogue, idea generation and relational modelling to help groups deal with complex issues.

nodes.label: Interactive Planning
nodes.description: Interactive Planning is Russell Ackoff's participative approach to redesigning a system by formulating its mess, developing an idealised design and planning how to move towards it.

nodes.label: Mosaic Transformation
nodes.description: Mosaic Transformation is a systemic approach to large-scale change that sequences mutually supporting packets of change, using complexity, variety and viability to avoid treating transformation as one centrally driven programme.

nodes.label: Multi-methodology including SOSM
nodes.description: Multi-methodology combines methods deliberately rather than treating one approach as universally sufficient. The System of Systems Methodologies is one influential framework for selecting approaches in relation to problem context and assumptions.

nodes.label: Patterns of Strategy
nodes.description: Patterns of Strategy is a systemic approach to strategy that models the changing fit and relationships among an organisation, competitors, partners, regulators and markets, supporting real-time strategic manoeuvring.

nodes.label: Socio-Technical Systems
nodes.description: Socio-technical systems thinking studies the joint design and interaction of social organisation, work, people and technology rather than optimising the technical system in isolation.

nodes.label: Soft Systems Methodology (SSM)
nodes.description: Soft Systems Methodology is a participative learning process for messy, contested human situations. It uses rich pictures, purposeful activity models and structured comparison to support inquiry and feasible change.

nodes.label: Strategic Options Development and Analysis (SODA)
nodes.description: Strategic Options Development and Analysis uses cognitive mapping and facilitated group work to structure a complex issue, surface differing interpretations and develop strategic options.

nodes.label: Syntegration / Team Syntegrity
nodes.description: Team Syntegrity is Stafford Beer's democratic large-group process for organising intensive, non-hierarchical dialogue around a shared issue using a highly structured pattern of roles and conversations.

nodes.label: System Dynamics
nodes.description: System Dynamics models behaviour over time through stocks, flows, feedback loops, delays and non-linear relationships. It is used to test explanations and policies through qualitative and quantitative simulation.

nodes.label: Systemic Intervention
nodes.description: Systemic Intervention combines critical reflection on boundaries with methodological pluralism and action. It treats intervention choices as practical, political and ethical rather than technically neutral.
nodes.canonical_definition: A systemic methodology that begins with critical reflection on boundaries and values, then draws on methodological pluralism to support responsible action in complex situations.

nodes.label: Viable System Model (VSM)
nodes.description: The Viable System Model is a management-cybernetic model for examining the functions and communications through which an organisation maintains autonomy, coordination, intelligence, identity and adaptation across recursive levels.
nodes.canonical_definition: A management-cybernetic model for diagnosing and designing the functions and communications by which an organisation maintains viable autonomy and cohesion in a changing environment across recursive levels.

nodes.label: Alan Turing
nodes.description: Mathematician whose 1936 paper formalised computability through the machine now bearing his name. It is context for recursive-function theory, not evidence that Turing originated recursion.

nodes.label: Archimedes
nodes.description: Ancient Greek mathematician whose work included iterative and self-referential constructions later compared with recursive ideas. The atlas currently treats this as historical comparison, not direct lineage to modern recursion theory.

nodes.label: Arturo Rosenblueth
nodes.description: Physiologist and co-author of the 1943 account connecting purposive behaviour, input/output relations and negative feedback.

nodes.label: Claude Bernard
nodes.description: French physiologist whose account of the stable internal environment influenced later work on physiological regulation and homeostasis.

nodes.label: Claude E. Shannon
nodes.description: Mathematician and electrical engineer whose 1948 paper established mathematical information theory and a general model of communication under uncertainty and noise.

nodes.label: David Hilbert
nodes.description: German mathematician whose work on formal foundations, geometry and mathematical problems shaped the context from which twentieth-century logic and computability developed.

nodes.label: Eilhard von Domarus
nodes.description: Psychiatrist and philosopher included because a contemporary historical lead proposes a connection to Warren McCulloch. The line remains provisional pending primary-source corroboration.

nodes.label: Francisco Varela
nodes.description: Chilean biologist and cybernetician who developed work on autopoiesis, cognition and second-order cybernetics with Humberto Maturana and others.

nodes.label: Gerald Midgley
nodes.description: Systems researcher associated with systemic intervention, boundary critique, methodological pluralism and the study of marginalisation.

nodes.label: Giuseppe Peano
nodes.description: Italian mathematician and logician known for axiomatic work on arithmetic and formal notation, part of the historical context for recursive definition.

nodes.label: Gregory Bateson
nodes.description: Anthropologist and cybernetic thinker whose work connected communication, learning, ecology, relationship, purpose and epistemology.

nodes.label: Harold Stephen Black
nodes.description: Bell Labs engineer whose 1934 paper set out the theory and engineering use of stabilised negative feedback amplifiers.

nodes.label: Heinz von Foerster
nodes.description: Austrian-American physicist and cybernetician associated with the Biological Computer Laboratory, self-organisation, the observer and second-order cybernetics.

nodes.label: Herbert Simon
nodes.description: American scholar of organisations, decision-making, artificial intelligence and complex systems; his work on near-decomposability and the architecture of complexity remains influential.

nodes.label: Humberto Maturana
nodes.description: Chilean biologist and cybernetician whose work on autopoiesis, cognition, language and the biology of knowing helped reshape second-order cybernetics.

nodes.label: Igor Perko
nodes.description: Systems and cybernetics researcher whose 2026 community map is retained as a comparator and discovery source.

nodes.label: James Clerk Maxwell
nodes.description: Physicist whose 1868 analysis of centrifugal governors is a historical precursor to mathematical control and feedback analysis.

nodes.label: Julian Bigelow
nodes.description: Julian Bigelow was an engineer and mathematician who co-authored the 1943 paper 'Behavior, Purpose and Teleology' with Arturo Rosenblueth and Norbert Wiener, an important precursor to early cybernetics.

nodes.label: Kurt Gödel
nodes.description: Kurt Gödel was a logician whose work on completeness, incompleteness and set theory transformed mathematical logic. Later systems writers sometimes extend his results metaphorically; those extensions require separate argument.
nodes.public_stub_text: Research stub. Kurt Gödel is included because it appears in one of the mapped source sets, but a reliable public explanation has not yet been written.

nodes.label: Leonardo of Pisa
nodes.description: Medieval Italian mathematician, also called Fibonacci, whose recurrence sequence is an early and widely used example of a recursively specified pattern.

nodes.label: Noam Chomsky
nodes.description: Linguist whose generative-syntax work is part of the linguistic-recursion research queue. The inherited edge remains unverified in this release.

nodes.label: Norbert Wiener
nodes.description: Mathematician and co-author of the 1943 teleology paper; later named and developed cybernetics as control and communication in animals and machines.

nodes.label: Panini
nodes.description: Ancient Sanskrit grammarian whose highly systematic generative rules are often discussed in histories of formal grammar. Retrospective comparison does not by itself establish direct influence on modern recursion theory.

nodes.label: Pingala
nodes.description: Ancient Indian scholar associated with combinatorial patterns in prosody, including recurrences later compared with binary and Fibonacci-like structures. Direct lineage claims require caution.

nodes.label: Plato
nodes.description: Ancient Greek philosopher included in the inherited recursion map through later traditions of forms and self-reference. The connection is presently historical comparison rather than demonstrated lineage.

nodes.label: Richard Dedekind
nodes.description: Mathematician reported by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy as an early formal user of definition by recursion in 1888. Primary-source checking remains outstanding.

nodes.label: Roger C. Conant
nodes.description: Roger C. Conant was a cybernetician who co-authored the 1970 good regulator theorem with W. Ross Ashby, linking effective regulation to a model of the system being regulated under stated formal assumptions.

nodes.label: Stafford Beer
nodes.description: British cybernetician and management thinker who developed the Viable System Model, Team Syntegrity and a practice of organisational cybernetics concerned with managing complexity and preserving operational autonomy.

nodes.label: Thoralf Skolem
nodes.description: Logician whose 1923 work linked recursive definability with effective computability, according to the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Primary-source checking remains outstanding.

nodes.label: W. Ross Ashby
nodes.description: Cybernetician who developed the Law of Requisite Variety and wrote An Introduction to Cybernetics.

nodes.label: Walter B. Cannon
nodes.description: Physiologist whose 1929 article developed the concept and terminology of physiological homeostasis.

nodes.label: Warren McCulloch
nodes.description: American neurophysiologist, philosopher and cybernetician whose work on neural nets, logic and cognition helped shape the Macy cybernetics community.

nodes.label: Quality management
nodes.description: Quality management organises work to meet and improve requirements and value over time. Systems approaches emphasise process behaviour, customer purpose, learning and management responsibility rather than inspection alone.

nodes.label: Systems | complexity | cybernetics
nodes.description: The deliberately overlapping field of inquiry and practice covered by this project.

nodes.description: Professional-body gateway to a searchable cybernetics library; use as a discovery corpus, not as evidence of claim correctness.

nodes.description: Biography by Ashby's daughter Jill, using Ashby's autobiographical notebook, family research and memories. It dates development of requisite variety to 1952–1953 and the writing of An Introduction to Cybernetics to 1952–1956.

nodes.label: An Introduction to Cybernetics
nodes.description: W. Ross Ashby, Chapman & Hall / John Wiley, 1956. Chapters 7–11 develop variety, information, regulation and the Law of Requisite Variety. Official Ashby archive bibliography records the first edition and a public PDF.

nodes.label: Principles of the Self-Organizing System
nodes.description: W. Ross Ashby, in Principles of Self-Organization, pp. 255-278. A primary cybernetic treatment stressing that organisation depends on distinctions and observer description.

nodes.label: Steps to an Ecology of Mind
nodes.description: Gregory Bateson's collected essays spanning cybernetic explanation, learning, communication, conscious purpose, ecology and form.

nodes.label: Stabilized Feedback Amplifiers
nodes.description: H. S. Black, Bell System Technical Journal 13(1), pp. 1–18. Primary engineering account of the negative-feedback amplifier principle. The invention predates the paper; this release does not make a first-invention claim.

nodes.label: Organization for Physiological Homeostasis
nodes.description: Walter B. Cannon, Physiological Reviews 9(3), pp. 399-431. Primary article establishing the physiological homeostasis formulation. This release uses bibliographic and article-level evidence and does not reduce homeostasis to feedback.

nodes.description: Core complexity-science concepts and methods: dynamics, chaos, fractals, information theory, self-organisation, agent-based modelling and networks.

nodes.description: Roger C. Conant and W. Ross Ashby, International Journal of Systems Science 1(2), pp. 89–97. The theorem concerns the simplest optimal regulator under stated assumptions and a mapping sense of model; popular summaries often omit these qualifications.

nodes.description: Family-tree map originated by Eric Schwarz; extended in 1998, 2000-01 and 2016.

nodes.label: Computing a Reality: Heinz von Foerster's 1973 lecture
nodes.description: A reconstructed 1973 lecture that developed into On Constructing a Reality; useful for observer-included epistemology and the construction of stable worlds through action and distinction.

nodes.label: On Self-Organizing Systems and Their Environments
nodes.description: Heinz von Foerster, Self-Organizing Systems, pp. 31-50. Public transcription of the primary chapter; useful for the system-environment and order-from-noise arguments.

nodes.label: Cybernetics or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine
nodes.description: Norbert Wiener's foundational synthesis, first published in 1948. The MIT Press open-access reissue describes feedback and information as central to the field. Exact chapter-level use remains a next editorial check.

nodes.label: Machine governors
nodes.description: Mechanical governors regulate machine speed by sensing motion and altering input. Their analysis provided an important historical route into mathematical control and later feedback concepts.

nodes.label: Behaviour over time graphs
nodes.description: A behaviour-over-time graph sketches how one or more variables change across a chosen period, helping an inquiry move from isolated events to patterns and possible dynamics.

nodes.label: Context diagrams
nodes.description: A context diagram shows a system of interest and selected exchanges with its environment, making the chosen boundary and external relationships discussable.

nodes.label: Enablers and inhibitors
nodes.description: An enablers-and-inhibitors analysis identifies conditions that support or obstruct a desired pattern of action, rather than assuming that outcomes follow directly from plans.

nodes.label: Identify leverage
nodes.description: Leverage analysis looks for places where a change in structure, information, rules, relationships or purpose may alter wider system behaviour.

nodes.label: Map analysis and narrative
nodes.description: Map analysis and narrative uses a visual systems map together with a written explanation, preventing the diagram from being treated as self-explanatory.

nodes.label: Monitoring and evaluation strategy
nodes.description: A monitoring and evaluation strategy specifies what will be observed, by whom, for what decisions and how learning will alter action as conditions change.

nodes.label: Pig model
nodes.description: The Pig Model appears in the UK government introductory systems toolkit. This atlas needs a fuller public explanation tied to the original toolkit before presenting it as complete.

nodes.label: Rich picture
nodes.description: A rich picture is an open, visual representation of a messy situation that can include people, structures, tensions, processes, emotions and differing perspectives without forcing them too early into one formal model.

nodes.label: Stock and flow diagrams
nodes.description: A stock-and-flow diagram represents accumulations, rates of change and the relationships controlling those rates, usually as part of System Dynamics.

nodes.label: Systems mapping
nodes.description: Systems mapping is a family of practices for making selected elements, relationships, feedback and boundaries visible so that participants can inquire into them together.

nodes.label: Theory of Change maps
nodes.description: A theory-of-change map sets out how activities are expected to contribute to intermediate conditions and outcomes, along with assumptions and evidence that can be tested.

nodes.label: Chaos theory
nodes.description: Chaos theory studies deterministic dynamical systems whose trajectories can show sensitive dependence on initial conditions, placing strong limits on detailed prediction while still allowing structural analysis.

nodes.label: Control theory
nodes.description: Control theory studies how dynamical systems can be regulated or guided through models, sensing, feedback, feedforward and designed action under disturbance and uncertainty.

nodes.label: Cybernetics
nodes.description: Cybernetics studies regulation, communication, circular causality, learning and purposive action in animals, machines, organisations and observers. It is a family of traditions rather than one settled doctrine.

nodes.label: Game theory
nodes.description: Game theory studies situations in which each participant's outcome depends partly on the choices of others, using formal representations of strategies, information, preferences and possible equilibria.

sources.title: American Society for Cybernetics online library
sources.notes: Professional-body gateway to a searchable cybernetics library; use as a discovery corpus, not as evidence of claim correctness.

sources.title: Biography: W. Ross Ashby (1903–1972)
sources.notes: Biography by Ashby's daughter Jill, using Ashby's autobiographical notebook, family research and memories. It dates development of requisite variety to 1952–1953 and the writing of An Introduction to Cybernetics to 1952–1956.

sources.title: An Introduction to Cybernetics
sources.notes: W. Ross Ashby, Chapman & Hall / John Wiley, 1956. Chapters 7–11 develop variety, information, regulation and the Law of Requisite Variety. Official Ashby archive bibliography records the first edition and a public PDF.

sources.title: Principles of the Self-Organizing System
sources.notes: W. Ross Ashby, in Principles of Self-Organization, pp. 255-278. A primary cybernetic treatment stressing that organisation depends on distinctions and observer description.

sources.title: Steps to an Ecology of Mind
sources.notes: Gregory Bateson's collected essays spanning cybernetic explanation, learning, communication, conscious purpose, ecology and form.

sources.title: Diagnosing the System for Organizations
sources.notes: Stafford Beer's guide to diagnosing organisations with the Viable System Model. The exact primary-book pages for the recursive-system theorem remain to be located before the organisational-recursion relation is promoted.

sources.title: Stabilized Feedback Amplifiers
sources.notes: H. S. Black, Bell System Technical Journal 13(1), pp. 1–18. Primary engineering account of the negative-feedback amplifier principle. The invention predates the paper; this release does not make a first-invention claim.

sources.title: Organization for Physiological Homeostasis
sources.notes: Walter B. Cannon, Physiological Reviews 9(3), pp. 399-431. Primary article establishing the physiological homeostasis formulation. This release uses bibliographic and article-level evidence and does not reduce homeostasis to feedback.

sources.title: Why I hope we could do better than the Castellani complexity map
sources.notes: Benjamin P Taylor's public critique is evidence of the design problem and the curator's position, not independent validation of The Necessary Tangle. It is paired with the original comparator in issue 6.

sources.title: The Atlas of Social Complexity
sources.notes: Major comparator for social complexity; maps achievements and possible directions.

sources.title: Aspects of the Theory of Syntax
sources.notes: Noam Chomsky's book is retained for the linguistic-recursion research queue. No settled influence or origin claim is made in this release.

sources.title: Introduction to Complexity (Santa Fe Institute Complexity Explorer)
sources.notes: Core complexity-science concepts and methods: dynamics, chaos, fractals, information theory, self-organisation, agent-based modelling and networks.

sources.title: Every Good Regulator of a System Must Be a Model of That System
sources.notes: Roger C. Conant and W. Ross Ashby, International Journal of Systems Science 1(2), pp. 89–97. The theorem concerns the simplest optimal regulator under stated assumptions and a mapping sense of model; popular summaries often omit these qualifications.

sources.title: Core Thinking Integration

profiles.title: Adaptation
profiles.canonical_definition: Change in a system's organisation, behaviour or relations that improves or preserves its capacity to remain viable in a changing environment.
profiles.summary: Adaptation is relational: change is adaptive only with respect to some environment, timescale and viability condition. Local adjustment can make the larger system more fragile.
profiles.why_it_matters: Transformation programmes often demand change without specifying what environmental variety has changed or what identity must be preserved. The result is motion rather than adaptation.

profiles.title: Autonomy
profiles.canonical_definition: The operational freedom and regulatory capacity of a part to respond to its local environment without being reduced to a passive execution point of the whole.
profiles.summary: Autonomy is not independence. A viable part needs discretion, information and resources, while remaining connected to wider identity and constraints.
profiles.why_it_matters: Local variety usually outruns central knowledge. Suppressing autonomy can make the whole legible to the centre while making it less able to respond where the work happens.

profiles.title: Boundary
profiles.canonical_definition: A purpose- and observer-dependent distinction that marks what is treated as inside, outside or marginal to a system of concern and thereby shapes explanation, legitimacy and intervention.
profiles.summary: A boundary makes inquiry and action possible by limiting what must be handled at once. It also externalises people, effects and responsibilities. Good systems work therefore treats boundary choice as practical, political and ethical.

profiles.title: Self-organisation
profiles.canonical_definition: A process in which interactions among components generate or maintain an organised macro-pattern without a central external controller prescribing that pattern; the system boundary, local rules, constraints and environment must be specified.
profiles.summary: Self-organisation describes organised macro-patterns arising through interactions among components rather than being prescribed by an external central controller. The system still depends on boundaries, local rules, resources, constraints and an environment.
profiles.why_it_matters: The phrase is often instrumentalised as if leaders can order emergence or simply withdraw. A useful account specifies the local interactions, constraints and selection processes that generate the pattern, and asks who drew the system boundary.

profiles.title: Systemic Intervention
profiles.canonical_definition: A systemic methodology that begins with critical reflection on boundaries and values, then draws on methodological pluralism to support responsible action in complex situations.
profiles.summary: Systemic Intervention refuses the idea that the problem and method are already given. It asks how boundaries and values create marginalisation, then selects and combines methods in relation to the situation.
profiles.why_it_matters: Method choice is itself an intervention. Boundary critique helps practitioners see whose concerns, knowledge and consequences are being made central or peripheral.

profiles.title: Transduction
profiles.canonical_definition: A boundary process that transforms signals, meanings or varieties from one domain into a form another domain can register and act upon; it is never assumed to be lossless.
profiles.summary: Transduction explains why a citizen's life becomes a case, a need becomes a code, work becomes a metric and strategy becomes a local instruction. The message is changed by the receiving world's categories and capacities.
profiles.why_it_matters: Transformation often fails at boundaries rather than within units. Seeing transduction reveals where meaning is lost, invented, protected or made actionable.

profiles.title: Variety
profiles.canonical_definition: The number of distinguishable elements or possible states in a specified set, sometimes expressed logarithmically; the distinctions and observer must be stated.
profiles.summary: Variety counts distinguishable possibilities. A system may have many physical states but little usable variety if the observer cannot distinguish them or the regulator cannot select among effective responses.
profiles.why_it_matters: Variety turns vague talk about complexity into a question about differences that matter for regulation. It also makes the observer visible: what counts as a different state depends on purpose, sensing and classification.

profiles.title: Variety amplification
profiles.canonical_definition: A deliberate increase in effective sensing or response variety available to a regulator, channel or operational unit.
profiles.summary: Amplification expands what a system can notice or do through capability, discretion, tools, coordination, networks and access to resources.
profiles.why_it_matters: When the environment cannot responsibly be simplified, the system must improve its repertoire. Giving people more cases without more authority or capability is workload amplification, not regulatory amplification.

profiles.title: Variety attenuation
profiles.canonical_definition: A deliberate reduction in effective variety so that relevant disturbances, signals or choices become tractable without pretending the discarded variety never existed.
profiles.summary: Attenuation protects a regulator from being overwhelmed. It can simplify, buffer, aggregate or redesign demand. It can also erase inconvenient people and conditions if the boundary and purpose are wrong.
profiles.why_it_matters: Forms, triage, standards, thresholds and dashboards are attenuation devices. Their value depends on whether they preserve the differences needed for responsible action.

profiles.title: Viability
profiles.canonical_definition: The capacity of a system to continue as a recognisable whole by balancing present operations, regulation, learning, adaptation and identity under changing conditions.
profiles.summary: Viability is not short-term survival or financial solvency. It concerns whether a system can keep producing itself as a coherent actor while its environment and internal conditions change.
profiles.why_it_matters: A viable organisation must handle today's work, disturbances and accountability while sensing and preparing for tomorrow. Central control cannot substitute for local regulatory capacity.

profiles.title: Viable System Model
profiles.canonical_definition: A management-cybernetic model for diagnosing and designing the functions and communications by which an organisation maintains viable autonomy and cohesion in a changing environment across recursive levels.
profiles.summary: The VSM is a model of the functions and communications needed for an organisation to remain viable in a changing environment. It distinguishes autonomous operations from meta-systemic functions for coordination, internal regulation, intelligence and policy, and applies recursively.
profiles.why_it_matters: The model makes the autonomy-cohesion problem explicit. It asks whether local operations can absorb relevant variety, whether conflicts are damped, whether the whole gains synergy, whether intelligence reaches strategy and whether identity closes the system without suffocating it.
